questions.topic: Radial colony growth from a spore
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of specific growth rate from colony area
questions.stem: Design a measurement, in lab-manual form, that lets a technician measure the specific growth rate of a fungal colony from its colony area on a plate.

answer.exemplar: Inoculate a plate at a single point, keep the temperature and agar constant, and measure the colony area at fixed intervals once the colony is in its exponential phase. Take the natural logarithm of each area, plot it against time, and read the slope, which is the specific growth rate because colony area doubles at a constant multiple.

questions.explanation: Colony area grows exponentially early on, so the slope of the log of area against time gives the specific growth rate. Take the measurements in that phase, before the plate is exhausted.
questions.hint: Plot the log of colony area against time and read the slope.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a yeast cell produces a daughter cell by budding
questions.stem: For the corrected manual, explain how a yeast cell produces a new daughter cell by budding.

answer.exemplar: The mother cell grows, and its wall softens locally at one point where a small bump appears. The nucleus divides and one nucleus moves into the bud, which enlarges as the mother supplies it with cytoplasm and wall material. When the bud is nearly full size it separates, leaving a scar of old wall on the mother and a slightly younger daughter.

questions.explanation: Budding is asymmetric division, so the manual is wrong to describe the cell splitting into two equal halves. The daughter is the smaller new cell, and the mother keeps a scar where it separated.
questions.hint: The daughter is the smaller cell; the mother keeps a scar.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why yeast budding is not equal division
questions.stem: Why does a yeast cell not simply split into two equal cells the way a bacterium divides? Explain for the corrected manual.

answer.exemplar: A yeast cell grows and then pushes out a small bump of new wall at one point on its surface, and only the new bud receives cytoplasm while the mother keeps all of its original contents. Because the division of the cytoplasm is unequal, the two cells differ in age and in size.

questions.learningObjective: Explain repeated budding from a single mother cell
questions.stem: For the corrected guide, explain why a yeast cell can keep budding even though it never grows large itself.

answer.exemplar: The bud is built from material the mother exports, and when the bud separates the mother has lost only a small share of its contents, so it can bud again almost immediately. Each round leaves a permanent scar of old wall on the mother, and a scar-rich cell buds less often, which is why the mother eventually stops or dies. The daughter, in contrast, starts with a full complement of cytoplasm and can grow.

questions.explanation: The mother supplies the bud but keeps most of its contents, so repeated budding does not exhaust it at once. What accumulates is scar, and a mother with many scars buds less often.

questions.stem: A fungal culture doubles its cell number every 5 hours while it is in its exponential phase. If the culture starts with 1,200 cells, how many cells are present after 15 hours?
questions.explanation: Fifteen hours is three doubling times, so the count is 1200 times 8, which is 9600. Adding a constant number of cells each hour would be wrong, since the rate of increase itself rises.
questions.hint: Count the doubling times and multiply by two each time.

questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of specific growth rates between two species
questions.stem: Design a way, in manual form, to compare the specific growth rate of two fungal species from their colony areas on separate plates.

answer.exemplar: Inoculate each species at a single point on its own plate under the same conditions, and measure each colony area at fixed intervals during the exponential phase, when the colonies are still well inside the plate. Take the natural logarithm of the areas, plot them against time, and read the slope for each species. The two slopes are the specific growth rates and can be compared directly.

questions.explanation: The slope of the log of colony area against time is the specific growth rate, so plotting both species this way makes the comparison direct. Areas must come from the exponential phase.
questions.hint: Plot the log of area against time for each species.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why budding speeds up when sugar is available
questions.stem: Explain, for the revised manual, why a yeast cell in a warm, sugary broth grows faster than one in plain water.

answer.exemplar: Yeasts are heterotrophic, so they need organic carbon to build their own material and to make energy. In plain water there is nothing to use, so budding slows and the cell may simply sit at the bottom of the vessel. In a sugary broth the cells have a plentiful supply of fermentable sugar, and the release of carbon dioxide and alcohol from that fermentation supports both growth and the budding of new cells.

questions.explanation: Yeasts feed on ready-made organic compounds, so plain water offers nothing to use. A sugary broth supplies fermentable carbon, and the energy released powers new wall and cytoplasm.
questions.hint: Yeasts cannot photosynthesise, so they need organic carbon.

questions.learningObjective: Design an exercise that justifies using radius to compare growth
questions.stem: Design an exercise, in manual form, that shows why a colony's radius can be used to compare growth rate between two plates.

answer.exemplar: Grow the same species on two plates with different agar depths and measure the radius of each colony at the same times. Plot radius against time for both and compare the slopes of the straight portions. Because the colony extends outwards at a constant rate in that phase, the slopes give the extension rate directly, and any difference can be related to the condition that was changed.

questions.explanation: In linear growth the radius increases by a fixed amount in a fixed time, so the slope of a radius against time plot measures extension rate. It is fair for two plates if both are in linear phase.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why budding can continue without oxygen
questions.stem: Set out, for the manual, why a yeast cell can bud without oxygen while a growing mould cannot keep extending without air.

answer.exemplar: A yeast cell can ferment its sugar, converting glucose into alcohol and carbon dioxide and still gaining a little ATP, which is enough to build the wall and cytoplasm of a small bud. Hyphae are larger and their walls are more demanding, so they rely on aerobic respiration, where oxygen is the final acceptor in the mitochondrial chain. Without air the hyphae cannot make enough ATP to extend their tips.

questions.explanation: The claim that budding needs air is wrong, because a yeast can ferment sugar and make the ATP a bud needs. A hypha demands more energy and needs aerobic respiration, so it stops without air.
questions.hint: Compare the energy yield of fermentation and respiration.

questions.stem: Design an activity, in manual form, that shows whether a colony on a plate is growing at a constant radial rate or at a decreasing one.

answer.exemplar: Inoculate a single spore in the centre of a plate, keep the plate in one position, and measure the colony radius at regular intervals over several days. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a daughter cell outlives the mother in a bud chain
questions.stem: Describe, for the corrected manual, why the daughter cell from budding can grow on its own while the mother becomes exhausted.

answer.exemplar: The bud is given a full share of the mother's cytoplasm, its own nucleus and a new wall of its own, so once it separates it has everything it needs to make new wall and new cells. The mother has given away a share of its contents, keeps a scar where the bud pulled away, and will give away more on the next bud. After many rounds the mother is a scarred, slowly growing cell, while the daughters are fresh cells with a full complement of machinery.

questions.explanation: The daughter leaves with its own nucleus, cytoplasm and wall, so it has what it needs to grow alone. The mother has lost a share of its contents and carries a scar from each bud, so it slows.
questions.hint: Compare what each cell keeps after the bud separates.
